Beast Clash is a monster battle. Choose the order your monsters enter. One active fighter per side attacks while teammates wait on the bench. Some abilities let benched teammates help. Substitutions. The battle runs on its own. Tap a living teammate in your lineup at the bottom to switch it in. The switch happens after both fighters act. Wait four exchanges between switches; the bar shows the wait. An exchange is one round of actions. A chosen replacement acts at half strength on its first turn. Your coaching staff

Five coaches. The head coach and the two coordinators set the schemes your plays come from, the scout finds monsters and reports on opponents, and the trainer runs practice. A coach who likes the same scheme as your monsters gives a small edge.
Look at each role and what it does.
Hire one coach per role; the cost counts against your salary cap.
Welcome to your week

A season is 15 weeks: 14 games and a bye. Each week runs Monday to Sunday: scout monsters, battle one to sign it, train, study the opponent, set your plays, talk to the press, then play on Sunday. The big yellow button always says what is next. "Let the staff run the week" does the weekday chores for you.
Press the big yellow button: it opens today's job.
Finish the job and you come back here for the next day.
After the game

The box score shows who did what. Your monsters earn experience and get tired; practice adds a little more, Saturday's lineup check takes most of it off, and a bye clears it. Win and the standings climb; lose and the season moves on, no replays.
Scouting and signing
Monday: scouting
Choose a region for your scout to search. Each region has its own monster types. A better scout finds more prospects and reveals more of their ratings.
Pick a region whose element you want.
Read the prospects: position, overall (OVR) and the ratings your scout could see.
Ratings and potential

Each monster has twelve ratings. Only some matter at each position: accuracy helps a quarterback, not a receiver. OVR is its overall rating at its position. Potential shows how much it can still improve. A “?” means your scout has not seen that rating yet.
Compare OVR with your monster at the same position (the ⓘ button does it for you).
A young monster with high potential grows the most.
Tuesday: monster encounter

Choose one prospect for a 3v3 Beast Clash. It fights beside two wild companions matched to your club’s strength. Only the prospect can join your team. Win and it wants to sign. After a loss, it may refuse to hear a pitch. Its salary must fit under your cap.
Choose the prospect you want most.
Keep the automatic lineup or pick your three strongest healthy monsters: a stronger lineup wins more often, a weaker one never makes the companions easier.
Wild companions

Why 3v3: a monster in the wild runs with a pack, so you meet three. The prospect you chose leads; the other two are wild companions. They are never signable, never join the roster, and their strength follows your club: the three together sit a little below your best three. Your strongest lineup wins about four times in five; your weakest rarely wins.
Skip Encounter or Skip to Results?

“Skip the encounter” cancels Tuesday’s battle and chance to sign the monster. You lose nothing else. “Skip to results” still plays the battle, but shows the result right away. The winner and experience stay the same.
Beast Clash
How Beast Clash works

Choose the order your monsters enter battle. The front monster on each side attacks. Supports and some Disruptors can help from the bench. After a knockout, the next monster enters. Existing health and effects stay. Win by knocking out every enemy, or having more health after 30 exchanges. Each exchange is one round of actions.
Pick your monsters and the order they enter; your strongest healthy ones are suggested.
Watch the battle at the speed you like, or skip straight to the result: it is the same battle either way.
Elements and type edges

Every monster has an element (fire, water and so on). Some elements hit others harder: ▲ next to a monster means it hits the one in front of it harder, ▼ means softer. Every monster also has one move and an ability that can turn a battle.
Order of entry

Your lineup sets the order your monsters enter. The first fights until knocked out, then the next enters. Health and effects stay through the battle. Try starting with a type advantage and saving your toughest monster for last.
The pregame Clash
Before kickoff a 3v3 Beast Clash replaces the coin toss. The winner chooses: receive the opening kickoff, or defer and get the ball to start the second half.
Overtime
A tie after the overtime quarter is settled by a Beast Clash: 3v3 in the season, 5v5 in the playoffs. The football score stands; the Clash decides who gets the win.
Your first game

Football in one breath: the offense has four tries ("downs") to move the ball 10 yards. Make it and you get four more; reach the far end zone for a touchdown (6 points, plus a 1-point kick). Fail on fourth down and the other team takes over, which is why you usually punt or kick a field goal (3 points) on fourth. You coach, you do not steer: pick one of your six play cards, press Snap, and watch the monsters run it.
Key Moments or Full Coaching
Key Moments is recommended. It skips routine plays and lets you coach the important ones. Full Coaching lets you call every play and takes about twice as long. Change this in Settings at any time.
The clock

Each play uses a few seconds. If the clock was still running after the last play, time between plays comes off when you snap. A timeout stops it. Hurry-up uses less time at no extra cost. A spike stops the clock but uses a down. To protect a late lead, milk the clock or kneel.
Plays
Every play has a lesson: what it is for and what beats it. You do not need to know them all; your six on Friday are what matter.
Wednesday: training
Choose one training focus this week. Harder sessions give bigger rewards but risk injuries. Using the same focus three weeks in a row stops helping.
Pick the area your team is weakest in.
Thursday: scout the opponent
Study the opponent’s offense or defense. You will learn the exact six plays that side will use on Sunday. Use that report to choose plays that can beat them.
Friday: game plan
Choose six plays for your offense and six for your defense. Those are the only plays you can call on Sunday. Plays marked ✦ counter what you learned on Thursday. A mix of runs and passes is safest.
Start from the coordinators' plan (already filled in).
Swap in any ✦ plays: they counter what the opponent showed.

The press asks three questions. Spotlight a star or talk trash before a rival game; the answers make the headlines. Your lineup is checked here too: injured or tired starters are swapped automatically.
Sunday: game day
First the pregame Clash decides who gets the ball. On the field, the top monster in each position starts. Badges show who got a training (T) or media (+) lift today.
Your roster
Seven starters a side, plus package players for special situations. Tap a monster for its ratings, Temper and ability. Starters are set for you, and you can override any slot.
Starters are the top name at each position.
An injured monster cannot play; a tired one plays worse.
Injuries and fatigue

Games, practice, and battles make monsters tired. They recover on Saturday and during a bye week. Tired monsters play worse. Injured monsters must wait a set number of weeks and cannot play football or battle.
Levels and evolution

Games and battles give experience. Leveling up brings natural growth toward a monster’s rating limits. Spend saved training points on its card; Temper changes the cost of improving each attribute. Training points are added each offseason. Some monsters can evolve at certain levels into stronger forms. You choose when to evolve them.
Contracts and money
Contracts and the salary cap

Pay every monster and coach each season. Total pay must fit under the salary cap. If you go over it, the commissioner chooses who leaves. Deals last one or two seasons. When a deal ends, renew it, offer less, or let the monster or coach leave.
Check the cap bar: green means room.
Re-sign the monsters you need first.
Draft day

Every club takes three first-year monsters, worst record first. Scouted prospects show their ratings; the rest are a gamble on the public board rank. Rookies cost 70% of market for two seasons, the cheapest good players you will ever sign.
Look at the prospects your scout studied first.
Pick for a position with no backup, or the best monster you can see.
Trading draft picks

You can trade your draft picks with other clubs: ask for a player at a position, ask for better picks, or answer a club that calls you with an offer. A trade cannot be undone. A player who arrives brings his salary with him.
On the draft screen, "Shop this pick" asks clubs what they would give.
A club may also call you during the season; the offer lasts until the week ends.
The Board
The Board and your goal

Before each season, the Board estimates your wins by comparing your team’s overall rating with the league average. The safe goal is that estimate, rounded. The medium goal is the playoffs. A rebuilding club may instead need one new gym badge. The stretch goal is the Beast Bowl and counts double.
Read the forecast: it is your club against this league, not against a fixed number.
A rebuilding club is forecast low and asked for little; a contender is asked for more.
Board confidence and dismissal

Meet your goal to gain +1 confidence, or +2 for the title, and clear any negative score. Miss it to lose 1. At −1, your job is at risk. A second miss there ends the franchise, unless you finish within one win of the goal or at least match the forecast. That earns one final warning. Three missed seasons in a row always end the franchise.
The league

Thirty-two clubs, two conferences, eight divisions. Fourteen make the playoffs: in each conference the four division champions and three wild cards, with a week off for the top seed, then four rounds to the Beast Bowl. Twelve clubs are led by Gym Leaders: beat one for a badge on the road to the Hall of Fame.

How It Works
Let Me Show You Around
You run the club. I’ll show you one job at a time. You can skip the tutorial whenever you like.
Meet Your Team
Open a beast’s card. Position is its job. OVR is a quick rating; individual ratings tell you what it does best.
Know Your Beast
Read its ratings and ability. Temper affects how efficiently it trains. Check fatigue and injuries before picking starters. ??? means you have not learned that information yet.
Choose a Starter
Tap a position, then start a different healthy beast at that position. Starters play first; backups fill in. You can change your choice back later.
Meet Your Coaches
Your head coach leads the team. Coordinators supply plays. Your scout finds prospects, and your trainer helps beasts improve. Review your staff; replacing anyone costs cap room.
Your First Draft
You have a draft pick before the week begins. Open the draft room, compare prospects, and choose who helps your club. Check the salary before confirming.
Choose Your Goal
Meet the Commissioner to choose a season goal. Reaching it builds the Board’s trust. Repeated misses can cost your job. Choose a goal you think you can reach.
Monday: Scouting
Choose a region to scout. Check your needs and the scout’s strengths. The results become Tuesday’s recruiting choices.
Tuesday: Recruiting
Compare a prospect with your team using its info button. ??? means unknown. Check salary and roster space. You may try to recruit a beast or leave it; you do not have to sign anyone.
Beast Clash Basics

Beasts fight automatically. Choose the team and order before starting. Type edges help some matchups. In Watch, tap an available reserve to request a switch at the next legal break. Abilities activate by their own rules; check each beast’s ability card.
Wednesday: Training
Choose an intensity and a training focus. Compare the success chance and injury risk before deciding. Training helps beasts grow. Resting skips today’s training benefits.
Thursday: Know Your Opponent
Scout their offense or defense. Read the report and look for a strength to stop or a weakness to attack. You will use this when choosing plays tomorrow.
Friday: Pick Your Plays
Choose your offensive and defensive plays. Offense moves the ball; defense stops it. Use yesterday’s report. Remove a selected play to make room, then save both sides of your plan.
Saturday: Media Day
Choose your answers at the press conference. Check the boosts and risks. Before moving on, review the lineup for injuries and tired beasts.
Sunday: Game Day
Check your starters and open today’s game. The opening Beast Clash decides who chooses possession. Once football starts, you’re in charge.
Learn From the Result
Win or lose, review the final score, stats, and rewards. A loss does not mean you did everything wrong. Look for one thing to improve.
Your Turn
Prepare for next week: inspect your team and make a lineup decision yourself. Keep your starters or change them. Use Help Me if you need a reminder.
Ready for Next Week
You have handled a full week. Use the day card to find your next job. Your Guidebook keeps these lessons, and I’ll explain new features when they appear.

Football: Your First Game

Score more points than the other team. A touchdown is worth 6 points. Your offense has four downs (plays) to gain 10 yards and earn four more. The first-down line shows the target. Choose a play, then use the controls shown on screen.
Move the Ball
Runs carry the ball. Pass plays send receivers along routes. Choose a play for the yards you need, then snap. Follow the controls for your selected mode; open match Help for the full control guide.
Stop Their Offense
Choose a defensive play, then start the play. Try to stop the runner or cover receivers. Watch the result to see the yards allowed. An interception or recovered fumble can give your team the ball.
Fourth Down
This is your last down. Going for it risks giving the other team the ball here. A punt kicks it farther away. A field goal tries for 3 points; distance affects the chance.
Kicks and Extra Points
Kickoffs start a possession. After a touchdown, choose a kick for 1 extra point or try a play for 2. Read the available choices before confirming.
Read the Play Result
Check the yards gained, the next down, and the score. One failed play does not decide the game. Use what happened to help choose your next play.
Abilities and Status Effects
Abilities can change what happens on a play. Tap a beast or an ability notice to inspect it. Status effects are temporary; the detail card explains what changed.
An Injured Beast
Open Roster and check who is out. A healthy backup at the same position can fill in. Check the lineup warnings before the next game.
Evolution
A beast is ready to evolve. Open its card and review the new form before confirming. You can return to this lesson in your Guidebook.
The Offseason
Review the season and Board result. Then handle expiring contracts, free agency, the draft, and roster preparation. Check salaries and cap room before each commitment.

Downs
Four tries to gain 10 yards. Make it and you get four more; reach the end zone for a touchdown (6, plus a 1-point kick). On fourth down you usually punt or kick a field goal (3).
The clock

The clock does not run while you choose a play. Each play uses a few seconds. If the last play ended with the clock running, time between plays comes off when you snap: {normal} s at normal tempo, {hurry} s in hurry-up, or {milk} s when milking the clock. Check the line under the score. An incomplete pass, run out of bounds, score, or timeout stops the clock. The next snap then uses no time between plays.
Timeout · Spike · Kneel · Tempo

Timeout: you have three each half. It stops the clock, so the next snap uses no time between plays. Use one on defense to stop an opponent running down the clock. Hurry-up cuts time between plays to {hurry} s. Milk clock raises it to {milk} s. Spike stops the clock but uses a down; it appears under a minute. Kneel uses time when you lead. With no enemy timeouts and less than {milk2} s left, kneeling ends the game.
Calling plays

Pick one of your six Friday play cards, then press Snap. On defense, pick a defensive play. ★ marks your coach’s suggestion. ✦ marks a play that counters your scouting report. A gray card needs players you cannot put on the field. FG tries a field goal on any down if it is in range.
Key Moments · Full Coaching · Auto · Sim

Key Moments skips routine plays and stops for important ones. Full Coaching lets you call every play. Auto picks plays for you at 1× or 2× speed until you stop it. Sim to key moment skips to the next important play. Sim to final finishes the game at once.
Edges

Scheme lock: all starters on a side fitting the coordinator's scheme play with +{schemeLockEdge}. Training (T) and media day (+) lifts show on the pregame lineup. Abilities fire on the strip under the field. Inspect: before the snap, tap a monster in the formation (or an entry of the ability strip) for its stamina, status and ability, and what is protecting it.
Type matchups

Before the snap, green ▲ means a good type matchup and amber ▼ means a tough one. Tap a matchup to see who may face whom. The edge helps only when those monsters actually meet. A different play or coverage can change the matchup. Ratings, plays and abilities still matter.

Owner or source
These words name the monster that creates the ability or effect. A rule about another effect’s source refers to the monster that created that other effect.
Qualifying, eligible, and legal
The play, monster, or action must meet the requirements listed in that rule. These words do not promise that an effect will work.
Normal damage and modifiers
Normal damage is the starting attack amount. A modifier changes that amount or another value. Type matchups, shields, and protection can still change the final result.
Queue, commit, and resolution
Queued means waiting to happen. Commit means the ability has been used up, even if its later effect fails. Resolution means finishing the action and its effects.
This monster
The monster whose ability you are reading. A teammate is on its side. A target is the monster the rule selects.
Turn and exchange
A turn is one monster’s regular chance to act. An exchange is a round of actions. These are different timers.
Attack and reaction
A normal attack uses a regular action. A reaction happens because something else happened, such as a hit. A reaction does not count as another regular turn.
Bench
Monsters waiting to enter battle. A rule may pause while its monster is on the bench.
Ready and recharge
Ready means the ability can be used if its requirements are met. The recharge rule tells you when it becomes ready again.
Status and one-effect rule
A status is a helpful or harmful effect. A monster normally has one at a time. A different effect can block a new one. Rules for refreshing or replacing the same effect still apply.
Guarded, Shielded, and Empowered
Guarded lowers damage taken. Shielded absorbs damage with a shield. Empowered raises damage dealt. These are different kinds of protection or help.
Scrimmage play
A regular football play that starts at the line of scrimmage. A kickoff, punt, or field-goal attempt is special teams instead. A rule says if two-point tries count.
Numbers separated by /
Read the numbers in order for the forms or mastery levels named in that rule. For example, 5 / 4 / 3 / 2 means the wait gets shorter at each listed mastery level.
Chance and percentage points
A chance is not a promise. Adding 5 percentage points to a 60% chance makes it 65%, not 63%.

The field
100 yards long, an end zone at each end. Your offense attacks up the screen toward the far end zone.
Downs
The offense gets four plays (downs) to gain 10 yards. Gain them and the count resets. “2nd & 7” means second down, 7 yards still needed.
Scoring

Touchdown: carry or catch the ball in the end zone, 6 points, then a 1-point kick. Field goal: kick it through the posts, 3 points, usually on fourth down when you’re close. Safety: tackled in your own end zone, 2 points to the other team.
Fourth down
Too far to go? Punt: kick it away so the other team starts far from your end zone. Close enough? Kick the field goal. Feeling brave? Go for it.
Positions (7 a side)
Offense: QB throws or hands off; RB runs; WR catch; TE blocks and catches; OL block. Defense: DL rush the passer and stop runs; LB do a bit of everything; CB cover receivers; S the last line.
Turnovers
Interception (defense catches a pass) or fumble (ball knocked loose and recovered): the other team gets the ball right there.
Attributes

Each monster has twelve attributes, such as speed, catching, and arm strength. Only some help at each position. Accuracy helps a quarterback, but not a receiver. Open More → What the stats mean to learn where training points will help. You can train any attribute, but not every attribute helps every position.
What you do
You don’t steer anyone. You build the team, pick the six plays for each side on Friday, and on Sunday you call one of those plays each snap. Monsters do the rest, using their ratings and abilities.

Flaroo treats sitting still as a problem that somebody else should solve. During timeouts it circles the bench, checks whether the next play has started, and circles the bench again just in case. Its bright ears and burning tail make it easy to spot; convincing it that warm-ups have ended is considerably harder.

Under the restless enthusiasm is a creature that wants to be useful. Flaroo celebrates a teammate’s first down with the same excitement as its own and takes a missed assignment personally. It is still learning that helping sometimes means waiting for the right moment instead of arriving at every moment at full speed.
Eager, affectionate, and impatient with absolutely anything that resembles a pause.
Its idea of resting between drills is a slower lap.
It has been known to celebrate the practice whistle before discovering that it means practice is starting.
Its first challenge is learning to direct its enthusiasm instead of spending all of it at once.
The extra lap
Learning the pause
Trust changes its behavior in small ways. Instead of pacing directly in front of a teammate during a difficult moment, it settles nearby. The tail still moves. The rest of it is trying very hard.
For all its movement, Flaroo keeps returning to the same spot beside its teammates. What it wants is not an endless run. It wants to know that, when the run is over, somebody has saved it a place.

Blazynx has discovered that waiting can be part of the chase. It watches a drill with a stillness that would have alarmed its younger self, then commits in one decisive burst. The old eagerness survives in the way it leans toward the field when its name is called.

It enjoys looking composed almost as much as it enjoys succeeding. A clean practice rep earns a measured nod; a compliment can undo the entire performance. Teammates learn to recognize the tiny preparations before it moves and the much less subtle pride afterward.
Focused and competitive, with a dignified manner that praise can unravel in seconds.
It will pretend that it was not waiting to hear the coach’s verdict.
Its impressive patience ends abruptly when someone suggests one more practice rep.
Restless enthusiasm becomes purposeful anticipation. It is learning to trust timing as much as effort.
Before the burst
Blazynx studies repetitions that once bored it. Its attention lingers on the instant before a teammate moves, as though it is trying to discover where a good decision begins.
The quiet challenge
It rarely announces a contest. It simply repeats a teammate’s drill a little more carefully and checks whether anyone noticed. Usually, everyone did.
Someone to follow
The first time a younger beast copies its routine, Blazynx becomes unusually deliberate. It has spent so long trying to look ready that being trusted to lead makes it want to be ready for real.

Infernox carries its energy with confidence instead of hurry. It no longer needs to be the first creature moving at every whistle. It surveys the group, finds its place, and makes that place feel dependable. Then the drill starts, and nobody mistakes its calm for a lack of enthusiasm.

Its protective streak appears in ordinary routines: waiting for the last teammate, repeating an exercise beside a discouraged rookie, and accepting congratulations only after checking who else deserves them. It still enjoys attention. It has simply become better at sharing it.
Steady, proud, and quietly protective; still delighted when the whole team joins the celebration.
It remains suspiciously available whenever a rookie needs a practice partner.
Its solemn pregame routine occasionally ends with the same impatient lean it had as a Flaroo.
The desire to belong matures into the confidence to make others feel that they belong.
The last teammate
Infernox finishes its work and looks back. If someone is still struggling, it makes its way over without turning the moment into an announcement.
Younger beasts sometimes gather around it before practice. It lets them imitate the serious parts of its routine and carefully overlooks their mistakes in the less serious parts.
The place it saved

Pebblit’s compact, plated outline causes a recurring misunderstanding during introductions: somebody assumes it will be easy to make room by moving it. Pebblit generally waits for the assumption to reconsider itself.

It enjoys a clear place in a shared routine and takes small promises seriously. Being underestimated irritates it less than being overlooked altogether. Familiar teammates discover a patient companion with an excellent memory for who asked before rearranging its afternoon.
Patient, particular about its place, and quietly amused by first impressions.
It chooses a resting place as though the decision matters.
Waits with immense composure while someone explains how easy this arrangement ought to be.
It begins saving a neighboring place for the companion who remembers to ask.
Pebblit learns that taking up space is not something it must defend at every introduction. A familiar team can recognize its place without another demonstration.
seems entirely comfortable with the place it has chosen.

Cobblon has grown into the presence its younger form once had to establish with patient persistence. It now watches introductions with the dry interest of a creature that has heard the obvious joke before.

It is particularly considerate about making space for someone smaller. The courtesy is practical rather than ceremonial: a clear place, an ordinary greeting, and no suggestion that the newcomer should be grateful for fitting. Its own confidence grows through offering what it once wanted.
Steady, dryly humorous, and considerate toward easily overlooked companions.
It notices when a small teammate has been left without a place.
Makes room before someone can deliver a grand speech about how considerate the gesture is.
It begins checking the gathering’s arrangement before settling into its own place.
Cobblon learns that an established place can become a welcome for someone else. Its steadiness begins to feel generous rather than merely difficult to question.
looks ready to make the arrangement comfortable for both of you.

Orogon carries its enormous presence without much need to announce it. The old patience survives in the deliberate pause before it joins a crowded routine and the attention it gives the smallest request for room.

It takes quiet pride in being a familiar landmark for its companions. That pride softens into genuine warmth when someone chooses its company for a reason unrelated to its imposing outline. The mountainlike impression is only the beginning of an unusually unhurried conversation.
Assured, welcoming, and quietly pleased to be chosen for company.
It remembers the resting places its oldest companions prefer.
Looks deeply satisfied when a tiny teammate treats its imposing arrival as completely ordinary.
It waits for a nervous newcomer to choose a place before settling nearby.
The small beast that once waited to be taken seriously has become a reassuring presence for others. Orogon learns that being dependable can also mean being easy to approach.
offers a patient welcome without making the moment feel small.

Craggo’s horns and determined posture suggest a creature that has never met an introduction it could not take seriously. It likes a clear task and can become wonderfully committed before considering whether it understood the details.

It values courage and occasionally confuses a patient pause with hesitation. A familiar coach can show it the purpose of waiting without making the lesson feel like a retreat. Its most useful discovery is that listening can be part of a determined beginning.
Brave, literal, and learning to put understanding before commitment.
It volunteers with impressive certainty before hearing every condition.
Begins an earnest demonstration, stops to ask a question, and looks proud of the improvement.
It begins repeating an instruction back before committing to the exercise.
Craggo learns that conviction can survive a clearer explanation. It becomes easier to rely on when its willingness to begin includes the patience to understand.
looks ready to take your next sentence very seriously.

Ramparte’s imposing posture is accompanied by a more deliberate attention than its younger form usually managed. It listens through the explanation before deciding where to put its considerable determination.

It has become patient with younger beasts who want to begin before they understand. Familiar companions recognize the quiet amusement behind its measured advice. The lesson it once needed is now something it can offer without making another creature feel foolish for needing it too.
Resolute, measured, and generous with practical patience.
It notices when enthusiasm has outrun an explanation.
Pauses before a serious instruction to make certain the youngest teammate has finished asking its question.
It begins helping a rookie sort an eager idea into a useful first step.
The old headlong conviction matures into dependable judgment. Ramparte learns to lend its courage to a companion without borrowing that companion’s choice.
gives your explanation its complete attention.

Bouldrox’s plated, horned outline supports a reputation for choosing the direct approach. It prefers an honest disagreement to a gathering full of elaborate hints and looks puzzled when the plain question is treated as impolite.

It is less interested in winning an argument than understanding why the group refuses to name it. A considerate companion helps it recognize that some creatures need time to find the words. Its directness becomes kinder when it makes room for that pause.
Plainspoken, purposeful, and learning the patience behind a gentle answer.
It asks the practical question before the ceremonial introduction is over.
Looks entirely pleased when a complicated debate finally becomes a clear request.
It begins waiting after a question instead of repeating it more firmly.
Bouldrox learns that a direct path can still include a considerate pace. Its clarity becomes something companions seek rather than something they prepare to withstand.
seems interested in getting to the plain and useful part of the conversation.

Granigor’s granite appearance makes a slow approach look monumental even when it is simply joining the equipment queue. It enjoys practical work and has little patience for a plan that nobody intends to carry out.

It can sound more severe than it feels, especially when asking an ordinary question. A familiar companion learns to hear the interest behind the plain manner. Granigor grows warmer in company when it notices that a small explanation can reassure someone without weakening the request.
Practical, steadfast, and gentler than its imposing outline suggests.
It prefers a useful task to a grand account of its strength.
Stops an impressive entrance to ask where the spare equipment belongs.
It begins explaining the reason behind a request rather than assuming it is clear.
Granigor learns that a dependable presence can be easy to approach. Familiarity turns its plain questions into the start of ordinary, welcome company.
looks ready for a clear question rather than an elaborate introduction.

Terrabull’s horns, plates, and broad presence give an ordinary change of position an unnecessarily dramatic appearance. It knows this and occasionally waits an extra moment before moving, just to see who notices.

Its humor is broader than its dignified pose suggests. It enjoys companions who can laugh at the spectacle without overlooking the care behind it. As trust develops, Terrabull becomes comfortable making a quiet entrance when somebody else needs the attention.
Imposing, playful, and quietly considerate beneath the spectacle.
It understands exactly how much attention its arrival attracts.
Pauses in a grand pose until a familiar teammate ruins the effect with an ordinary question.
It begins checking the group’s mood before choosing how dramatic an entrance to make.
Terrabull learns that a large presence can make room as readily as it can fill it. Its confidence becomes more enjoyable when the spectacle is shared by choice.
seems to be considering a slightly theatrical greeting.

Titanolith’s mountainlike outline and crown have earned it an audience before it has said anything. An ordinary practice visit can acquire the atmosphere of a public appearance, to its occasional and visible inconvenience.

It appreciates a companion who can see the practical creature behind the stories. A small request, a shared task, or an unremarkable rest can become welcome relief from admiration. Its quiet generosity is easiest to notice when nobody insists on describing it as legendary.
Patient, imposing, and grateful for ordinary companionship.
It enjoys helping with tasks that do not attract spectators.
Looks quietly delighted when a teammate forgets to make its arrival into an event.
It begins returning to the same small gathering where nobody rehearses the greeting.
The living mountain remains a grand story. Familiar company offers Titanolith something the story cannot: a place where it can be useful without being monumental.
appears pleased by an introduction without a ceremony attached.

Slatelet’s plated, flat-headed silhouette gives its patient expression a particularly solid appearance. It has a habit of waiting through a difficult explanation rather than pretending that the first confusing sentence was sufficient.

It enjoys a steady task and dislikes being hurried toward a solution nobody has explained. A familiar partner discovers a dry wit beneath the practical manner. Its confidence grows when it begins asking the group to match its clarity rather than silently enduring every muddled instruction.
Patient, plainspoken, and quietly skeptical of vague assurances.
It waits for the full explanation before agreeing that something is simple.
Offers an entirely practical question in the middle of an impressive but unhelpful speech.
It begins asking what the next step means instead of accepting a confident gesture.
It learns that patience need not mean absorbing every confusion alone. A clear question can make the entire gathering easier to understand.
looks ready to wait for a properly explained answer.

Gravelpup’s plated, puppyish outline makes its serious interest in another creature’s task look endearingly formal. It enjoys having a clear way to help and sometimes volunteers before anyone notices that it wanted an invitation.

It can overlook its own enjoyment while making sure the group’s work is covered. Familiar teammates help by asking what it would like to try for itself. Learning to accept that turn gives its helpfulness a more comfortable balance without taking away the pride behind it.
Helpful, earnest, and learning to make room for its own interests.
It notices an uncovered task before the group disperses.
Looks startled and delighted when somebody offers to handle its usual job for a change.
It begins waiting to see whether a teammate actually needs help before volunteering automatically.
Gravelpup learns that being valued is not the same as always being useful. Its place in the team can include an afternoon chosen simply because it would enjoy it.
seems interested in whether there is something useful it can share.

Mudlark’s sturdy, beaked outline can make an ordinary introduction feel unusually businesslike. It enjoys practical company and has a dry appreciation for teammates who get to the point without forgetting to be kind.

It dislikes being treated as a joke whose appearance supplies the entire punchline. Familiar companions discover a cheerful creature perfectly capable of enjoying the joke when it is allowed to help tell it. Trust grows when the group makes room for more than the obvious first impression.
Sturdy in manner, dryly cheerful, and appreciative of considerate humor.
It likes a useful task with a clear finish.
Waits for an obvious appearance joke to end, then improves the punchline.
It begins contributing its own humor instead of merely tolerating the introduction.
Mudlark learns that it can belong to the joke without being reduced to it. The group begins enjoying the companion as much as the memorable outline.

Springlet’s coiled, winged appearance makes a quick recovery from embarrassment look almost inevitable. It enjoys a lively practice and often looks ready to try again before anyone has finished commenting on the previous attempt.

It can hide disappointment behind another cheerful beginning. A familiar companion who asks the quieter question discovers that persistence does not prevent a task from feeling difficult. Springlet grows more comfortable when it can accept encouragement without first performing another demonstration of resilience.
Lively, persistent, and more sensitive than its ready smile suggests.
It starts preparing another attempt before the group has settled the last one.
Begins a cheerful restart, notices a patient companion waiting, and allows itself a proper pause.
It starts telling a familiar partner when an exercise has become frustrating.
Springlet learns that resilience can include taking time to feel disappointed. Its cheerful returns become more genuine when nobody expects every difficult moment to disappear immediately.
looks ready to turn the pause into another friendly beginning.

Anvilox’s horn and plated outline make a careful, ordinary arrival look much more workmanlike than it may have intended. It enjoys knowing which part of the day belongs to it and prefers a useful task to a noisy introduction.

It can become quietly resentful when its willingness is treated as the entire plan. A familiar companion helps it ask for a fair share of the rest as well as the work. Its confidence grows when reliability becomes something the team shares instead of something it praises from a distance.
Practical, conscientious, and quietly attentive to a fair division of effort.
It remembers the job still waiting after the celebration ends.
Looks delighted when somebody stays to share the final task without being asked.
It begins checking how the work is divided before accepting the familiar assignment.
Anvilox learns that being useful can lead into company rather than another obligation. A fair arrangement lets its generosity remain warm instead of merely dependable.
seems pleased by a conversation that begins with a clear and fair arrangement.

Kettlump’s dented shell and familiar whistle give its presence the reassuring character of well-used equipment. It likes an established resting place and has firm opinions about arrangements that look exciting but do not look comfortable.

It is more sociable than its settled posture suggests. A companion who sits nearby without proposing a relocation often receives an excellent account of the afternoon. Learning to explain a preference before turning it into a complaint helps Kettlump invite company without giving up its cherished comfort.
Comfort-minded, opinionated, and warmly conversational once settled.
It has a detailed assessment of the familiar resting places.
Considers a proposed move with an expression suggesting that an entire committee should first inspect the destination.
It begins inviting a teammate to share its favorite quiet corner.
Kettlump learns that comfort can include another creature’s preference. Its familiar place becomes more enjoyable when the arrangement is chosen together instead of defended alone.
looks pleased that the conversation does not require relocating immediately.

Ingotusk’s nearly square outline lends a satisfyingly definite appearance to its preference for a clear place and a clear task. It has little interest in being hurried toward an exciting idea whose purpose keeps changing.

It enjoys a companion who can distinguish firmness from hostility. Once the agreement is understood, its dry humor appears in small, practical observations. Ingotusk becomes more flexible when it knows that reconsidering one detail will not be mistaken for agreeing to everything else.
Firm, practical, and quietly funny about elaborate uncertainty.
It likes an assignment with a recognizable finish.
Responds to a dazzling new plan by asking which part is actually supposed to happen first.
It begins asking for one clear adjustment instead of dismissing the whole unfamiliar arrangement.
Ingotusk learns that an honest boundary can make cooperation easier. Its steadiness becomes a comfortable point of reference rather than a position the group expects to argue around.
looks ready for the plain and useful version of the explanation.
Brasshound’s familiar collar and attentive expression make a practical greeting look particularly earnest. It likes being part of a routine that somebody would notice becoming incomplete without it.

It is more vulnerable to disappointment than its willingness suggests. A familiar teammate learns to praise the careful work without pretending the mistakes were invisible. Brasshound grows when it can accept an honest account of the afternoon and still trust that its place in the group is secure.
Faithful, conscientious, and reassured by honest rather than extravagant praise.
It remembers who returns for the least glamorous part of practice.
Looks relieved when a teammate acknowledges a mistake and stays to help with the next attempt anyway.
It begins telling a familiar partner when it wants to repeat a difficult exercise.
Brasshound learns that belonging does not depend on an unbroken account of success. Trust makes it possible to keep trying without turning every mistake into a question about its welcome.
gives you an attentive and thoroughly sincere greeting.

Gyroflit’s unusual wings and steady posture make a careful wait look like a well-balanced demonstration. It enjoys a familiar sequence and is quietly proud when the whole arrangement remains calm around a difficult detail.

It can become uncomfortable when someone treats a deliberate adjustment as a failure to be lively. A considerate partner leaves room for the pace at which it does its best thinking. Gyroflit grows more sociable as it learns to explain that preference without expecting a debate about enthusiasm.
Measured, precise, and quietly appreciative of a considerate pace.
It checks a sequence before agreeing that a shortcut will improve it.
Looks deeply satisfied when a busy group finally discovers the usefulness of a measured pause.
It begins asking for the extra moment that makes an unfamiliar task clearer.
Gyroflit learns that steadiness can invite another creature in. Its preferred rhythm becomes a shared resource rather than a private defense against being hurried.
seems ready to consider the next step carefully.

Clockcrow’s upright, clockwork outline makes a punctual arrival feel almost official. It enjoys knowing when a gathering begins and becomes quietly interested in the reasons other creatures give for ignoring that useful information.

Its dry humor is easier to hear once teammates stop interpreting every practical reminder as a reprimand. Learning to ask whether someone needs help makes its orderly habits more welcoming. Clockcrow discovers that a well-kept routine can support a friendship without becoming the only subject available.
Punctual, dryly observant, and learning to put company ahead of the timetable.
It remembers the time that was actually printed on the invitation.
Offers a solemn reminder that turns out to contain an unexpectedly kind joke.
It begins waiting beside a familiar companion instead of watching the entrance alone.
Clockcrow learns that keeping time can include making room for someone else’s difficult day. Its reminders become warmer when they carry an invitation rather than a verdict.
appears pleased that there is time for an ordinary conversation.

Washerling’s small, plated shell gives a deliberate arrival the air of a carefully completed journey. It enjoys a steady preparation and dislikes being hurried through the part that makes the task feel understandable.

It is more interested in considerate company than an audience for patience. A familiar partner learns to begin the conversation where it is instead of calling from the destination. Washerling’s confidence grows when its own pace becomes part of a shared afternoon rather than an inconvenience to explain.
Deliberate, companionable, and reassured by a welcome that does not hurry it.
It likes a clear destination and an honest amount of time to reach it.
Looks delighted when a teammate chooses to share the journey rather than applaud the eventual arrival.
It begins inviting a companion into the quiet part of preparation.
Washerling learns that company can travel at its pace without making the afternoon smaller. Its reliability gains a warmer meaning when somebody values the creature as well as the arrival.
seems pleased by a greeting that meets it where it is.

Spriglet considers a bouncing object an invitation. A dropped ball, a rolling marker, or a teammate’s untidy practice equipment can all become the beginning of a very important investigation. Its leaflike ears turn toward the next distraction while the rest of it is still pursuing the last one.

Curiosity makes it a cheerful companion and an occasionally exasperating student. It wants to understand the drill, the equipment, and why the coach is hiding that interesting object behind a clipboard. Give it something specific to learn, and its wandering attention becomes surprisingly patient. It is proudest when it discovers that the answer can help a teammate.
Inquisitive, sociable, and convinced that almost everything deserves a closer look.
Among the paths and undergrowth of the Emerald Wilds, it investigates the small movements that other travelers pass without noticing.
It treats a familiar trail as if somebody may have added something interesting since yesterday.
Its early enthusiasm is about finding things; maturity will teach it to notice which discoveries matter.
One more question
Spriglet watches a teammate repeat a difficult drill, then tries it from the same spot. For once, the attraction is not the ball. It wants to understand what its teammate is trying to do.
After discovering something interesting, it often returns to the group before investigating further. Exploration has become more satisfying when there is somebody to share it with.
{name} notices something beside you, then checks whether you noticed it too.
{name} turns its leaflike ears toward the next interesting sound.
{name} brings its investigation to a halt. For the moment, you are apparently the most interesting thing here.

Floracat has learned to finish one investigation before beginning another. Usually. It follows a practice routine with an attentive expression, then returns to examine the detail that caught its interest earlier. Teammates recognize that look and check their equipment before it decides the mystery needs assistance.

The urge to explore has become an interest in patterns. It enjoys a well-repeated exercise and becomes quietly pleased when a small adjustment finally makes sense. It can grow impatient with vague instructions, but its questions rarely come from defiance. Floracat wants a reason it can carry into the next attempt.
Attentive and thoughtful, with a persistent need to know why.
It follows familiar trails through the Emerald Wilds, returning to places where the changing surroundings offer something new to observe.
It remembers which part of an explanation the coach skipped.
Curiosity becomes observation: it starts connecting separate discoveries instead of simply collecting them.
Floracat sometimes repeats a successful exercise slowly. It is not dissatisfied with the result; it wants to understand which part made the difference.
When another beast struggles with an instruction, Floracat asks a question that makes the explanation clearer for everyone. It looks faintly surprised when the teammate thanks it.
Room for an answer
It learns that a question can help someone think, but only if it leaves time for the answer. Its growing patience is easiest to see when it practices with younger beasts.
{name} studies you with the expression of someone preparing a very specific question.
{name} appears to solve a mystery, then looks mildly offended that nobody saw it happen.

Sylvanyx does not rush to fill a quiet moment. It observes the group, the exercise, and the small signs that someone has stopped following along. The same curiosity that once sent it chasing loose equipment now makes it attentive to the creatures around it.

Its calm is not solemnity. Sylvanyx enjoys a good surprise, and an unexpected bounce can still interrupt an otherwise dignified afternoon. It has simply learned that noticing something does not require pursuing it immediately. More often, it chooses a place beside the team and lets the next discovery come to it.
Perceptive and patient, with a playful curiosity beneath its composed manner.
The paths of the Emerald Wilds are familiar territory, but it remains alert to the quiet changes within them.
It occasionally follows a rolling ball farther than its dignified exit was meant to suggest.
Younger beasts mistake its patience for knowing every answer. It is remarkably tolerant of this arrangement.
Observation develops into understanding, and understanding becomes an instinct to make room for others.
The quiet observer
Sylvanyx can sit through a whole explanation without interrupting. Afterward it approaches the teammate who looked confused, rather than the coach who already understood it.
An old distraction
What stayed curious
The young creature that chased every movement has not disappeared. Its curiosity has grown large enough to include what teammates need, what they leave unsaid, and when they might welcome company.
{name} watches you patiently, as if there is no need to hurry the conversation.
{name} briefly abandons its composed pose to investigate a tiny distraction. It returns looking entirely innocent.

Cindruff arrives with soot on its coat and an opinion about whether it needs a break. The opinion is usually no. Its small stature does little to soften the stubborn set of its posture, and the faint smoky appearance tends to survive attempts to make it presentable for team photographs.

It dislikes being dismissed more than it dislikes difficult work. A patient coach can turn that determination into steady practice; an impatient one may discover that Cindruff has interpreted encouragement as a challenge. Under the bluster is a creature that wants its effort to count, especially when somebody stronger is watching.
Stubborn, earnest, and more sensitive to being underestimated than it wants to admit.
It is found around the Volcanic Fields and Thunder Plains, bringing the same persistent attitude to an exposed trail that it brings to a drill.
It can make the phrase “last rep” sound like a negotiation.
Its early determination is personal. Growing confidence will help it distinguish proving itself from doing what the team needs.
Still here
When a drill goes badly, Cindruff stays nearby until it has an opportunity to try again. It seems less concerned about the mistake than about being remembered for stopping afterward.
The sensible break
After enough time with a trusted team, it occasionally accepts a rest without an argument. It still positions itself where everyone can see that it intends to come back.
{name} straightens its posture as if you have come to inspect its effort.
{name} looks ready to insist that the last drill was only a warm-up.
{name} visibly relaxes for a moment, notices you watching, and resumes looking extremely busy.

Magmaul has stopped treating every instruction as a test of its determination. It still commits to work with an intimidating seriousness, but there is a new steadiness in how it listens before beginning. Teammates can suggest a different approach without first preparing for a debate. Most days.

Its protective side appears when somebody younger is being overlooked. Magmaul remembers the feeling and is reluctant to let another creature carry it alone. It may offer its help with a gruff expression, then remain long after the original exercise has finished. Being dependable has become more important than looking impossible to discourage.
Resolute and protective, with a dry patience that took considerable practice to acquire.
It remains at home in the Volcanic Fields and Thunder Plains, where its deliberate presence contrasts with its younger form’s restless insistence.
It can make a quiet nod feel like an unusually generous compliment.
Its advice about taking breaks is considerably more reasonable than its former opinions on the subject.
Determination matures into reliability. It learns to offer the reassurance it once wanted for itself.
Before the next rep
Magmaul watches a younger beast struggle and suggests beginning again together. It does not mention that it was once equally reluctant to accept help.
It becomes more willing to change a routine when the coach explains the purpose. Holding to a goal, it has discovered, does not require holding to every habit.
Someone who stays
The same stubbornness that once demanded another attempt now keeps Magmaul beside an exhausted teammate. It knows when encouragement should be a speech and when it should simply be company.
{name} acknowledges you with a steady nod.
{name} offers a small, unmistakably proud smile, then becomes very interested in the next practice assignment.

Pyroclast looks like the sort of arrival that should come with an evacuation plan. Dark plates, a glowing volcanic palette, and a formidable crown give it a presence that makes ordinary introductions feel underprepared. The familiar stories about ground glowing beneath the goal posts have done nothing to make its reputation quieter.

Its manner is more deliberate than the stories suggest. Pyroclast allows a conversation to reach it rather than competing to be heard. Around younger beasts, that patience can become an unexpected kindness: it waits through an awkward introduction as if there were no more important appointment in the world. The spectacle belongs to its reputation. Its attention belongs to whoever is in front of it.
Formidable and deliberate, with an unexpected patience for nervous company.
Associated with the Volcanic Fields, its dark plated silhouette and volcanic glow suit the landscape that surrounds its legend.
Teammates sometimes practice what they will say before introducing themselves.
It has a talent for making a short silence feel ceremonial.
The introduction
After the stories
Teammates who know it well speak less about its silhouette and more about the way it listens. This rarely improves the stories told by beasts who have not met it.
The smaller legend
{name} gives you its attention with unhurried solemnity.
{name} inclines its head as if your brief visit is an occasion deserving a ceremony.

Aquip approaches practice as an elaborate invitation to play. Its fins and whiskers give it a distinctive outline, but teammates usually recognize it by the expectant look that appears when someone changes direction. To Aquip, a route is a suggestion that the game of tag has begun.

It is sociable without being still for very long. A missed attempt can disappoint it, yet a willing partner usually restores its interest before the coach finishes explaining the mistake. The challenge is teaching Aquip that the rules are part of the fun. Once it understands the purpose of an exercise, it wants everyone else to enjoy getting it right too.
Playful, inviting, and inclined to mistake a serious expression for the beginning of a chase.
It is encountered around the Coral Coast and Shadow Marsh, where movement near the water attracts its attention.
It looks mildly betrayed when a partner announces that tag is finished.
Play becomes cooperation as it learns that a shared game needs shared rules.
Your turn
Aquip often returns toward a practice partner after a successful exercise. It appears to be checking whether they are ready to make the next attempt interesting.
The rules of the game
It begins to wait for the proper start of a drill instead of anticipating every movement. The waiting is visibly difficult. The success afterward seems to make it worthwhile.
Everybody included
When a teammate hesitates at the edge of a group exercise, Aquip makes room for another partner. It has come to regard a game that leaves someone out as an unfinished arrangement.
{name} watches for your next move with unmistakable enthusiasm.
{name} waits perfectly still for a moment, then looks delighted with its own astonishing restraint.

Aquarrel has learned to keep some of its excitement in reserve. It observes the start of a drill with an intent expression, waiting for the cue that turns attention into movement. The old delight returns as soon as the exercise begins. Its teammates recognize that competitive look and prepare for an energetic afternoon.

It still wants practice to be enjoyable, but now takes a poor effort rather personally. Learning to separate a disappointing repetition from a disappointing teammate is part of its growth. A clear conversation and another chance usually help more than a lecture. It cares about the partnership enough to keep trying.
Competitive and attentive, with a playful streak that needs occasional reminders about patience.
The Coral Coast and Shadow Marsh remain familiar surroundings; it spends more time watching the movement around it before joining in.
It can look unusually serious while waiting to do something it finds extremely fun.
It remembers which teammate last claimed a practice victory.
Its playful attention becomes competitive focus, and it begins learning how to share both success and frustration.
Keeping count
Aquarrel sometimes remembers a practice score nobody else realized was being recorded. It is persuaded to start a fresh contest more easily than to concede the old one.
After a frustrating session it returns to the same partner with a more patient approach. The rematch has become an opportunity to repair the mood, rather than merely settle the result.
It learns to celebrate an exercise in which its partner improves, even when that improvement makes its own task harder. Competition begins to feel more useful when both beasts leave stronger.
{name} gives you a focused look, as if considering the terms of a friendly contest.
{name} appears ready to announce a practice score, thinks better of it, and settles for an exceptionally pleased expression.

Abyssin has the attentive calm of a creature that no longer needs to begin every contest. It studies the group before joining an exercise and carries its enthusiasm without advertising every spark of it. A familiar teammate can still draw out the old playfulness with a change of direction and an inviting glance.

Its maturity appears in how it handles someone else’s difficult day. It can offer a demanding practice partner without turning the session into a judgment. The pleasure of competition remains, but it has become comfortable with a quieter result: the group understanding one another better at the end than at the beginning.
Composed, perceptive, and quietly playful with those it trusts.
It remains associated with the Coral Coast and Shadow Marsh, taking a measured interest in surroundings its younger forms hurried to explore.
It is particularly good at making a rematch feel like a fresh start.
Competition matures into trust. It learns to challenge a teammate without making that teammate feel alone.
The invitation
Abyssin occasionally waits at the edge of an exercise until a hesitant teammate joins it. What follows looks like ordinary practice unless someone notices who was invited first.
Without the score
It can finish a long session without asking who won. The quality of the exchange has become interesting enough to occupy its attention.
Still a game
{name} regards you calmly, with a hint of a familiar playful expression.
{name} briefly adopts its younger form’s expectant posture, then resumes looking impeccably composed.

Muddlet is heavy, happy, and remarkably committed to a comfortable position. Its rounded, ear-topped shape gives it a friendly appearance; the expression becomes even friendlier when it discovers that the next instruction involves staying where it is. Asking it to move usually produces a thoughtful pause before any visible agreement.

The pause should not be mistaken for indifference. Muddlet notices when a teammate needs room, company, or a calmer corner of the group. Its easy manner can make those gestures seem accidental, but it is surprisingly consistent about them. It enjoys belonging to a team and prefers to express that enjoyment without unnecessary hurry.
Contented, considerate, and inclined to give every change of plans a little thought.
Found around the Coral Coast and Shadow Marsh, it favors familiar resting places and the company of creatures willing to slow down beside it.
It considers a good resting place an important discovery.
Its agreement to move can begin with a very convincing impression that it has not heard the request.
Its comfort with staying put becomes an understanding of when another creature needs steady company.
The chosen spot
Muddlet sometimes settles beside a teammate before choosing the more comfortable empty space nearby. The choice is quiet enough to go unnoticed.
Making room
When the group grows crowded, it shifts without being asked. This is notable chiefly because the same request from a practice whistle can require lengthy consideration.
Teammates begin to regard its presence as part of the routine. Muddlet seems content with this arrangement: a dependable place in the group is one of its favorite kinds of comfort.
{name} looks pleased that you have decided to spend a quiet moment here.
{name} considers moving to greet you, decides the present arrangement is excellent, and looks warmly satisfied.

Sludgeon has developed a deliberate steadiness that makes its younger form’s contentment look almost energetic. It does not hurry to announce an opinion, but once it commits to a task the team can usually stop wondering whether somebody will see it through. Its unassuming manner hides a considerable pride in being relied upon.

It remembers the value of a comfortable place and has expanded its definition to include the creatures nearby. A teammate recovering from a rough session may discover that Sludgeon has quietly joined them. It rarely presses for conversation. It has learned that being dependable can mean remaining present until the other creature is ready to move.
Steady and quietly reassuring, with a patient pride in doing its part.
Its familiar territory remains the Coral Coast and Shadow Marsh, where it returns to well-known places with an unhurried confidence.
It can turn a pause into the most reassuring part of a difficult afternoon.
Comfort becomes reassurance: it learns that a steady presence can help the whole group find its balance.
Already there
Sludgeon often begins a familiar task before anyone asks who will handle it. It seems to appreciate being noticed, but does not interrupt the work to make certain that it is.
When it moves
The creature famous for staying put becomes the first to make space when a teammate needs it. Its patience was never simply a refusal to move; it was learning which movements were worth making.
{name} acknowledges your visit with an unhurried, contented expression.
{name} makes a small adjustment to leave you more room. Coming from this beast, it feels like a considerable welcome.

Mossmaw can remain quietly occupied beside practice long enough for others to forget it is listening. Its mossy mane and patient expression give a rest period the atmosphere of a comfortable woodland clearing.

It likes familiar company without requiring constant conversation. When it finally offers an opinion, the group usually discovers that it has been following every detail. Its growing confidence appears in the willingness to speak before somebody remembers to ask.
Patient, attentive, and comfortable with a companionable silence.
It returns to the shadiest familiar resting spot.
Offers a perfectly relevant observation after everyone assumes it was asleep.
It begins choosing a resting place close enough to hear a favorite teammate’s conversation.
Its patience becomes an invitation rather than a hiding place. Mossmaw learns that being quietly present can include making its own wishes heard.
seems quite content to share an unhurried moment.

Fungorilla’s larger presence has not displaced the old preference for a quiet place beside the group. It settles with deliberate care, making an ordinary rest feel as though somebody has finally called the gathering to order.

It has become more willing to interrupt when a teammate is overlooked. The words remain measured, but the intention is unmistakable. Its patience now includes the confidence to act, without treating every disagreement as an invitation to become loud.
Measured, protective, and quietly confident about making room for others.
It remembers who prefers a quieter corner after practice.
Pauses in the middle of a very serious discussion to enjoy an unexpectedly comfortable silence.
It speaks up for a teammate before the conversation moves past that creature’s concern.
What once looked like endless waiting becomes deliberate care. Fungorilla knows when to remain still, and when someone needs it to stand beside them.
gives you a slow, welcoming acknowledgment.
Bramblet examines a practice arrangement and chooses a position as though the decision will need to withstand several seasons. Its horned outline looks entirely at ease once the choice is made.

It appreciates consistency and occasionally needs reminding that an adjustment is not a betrayal of the original plan. A teammate who explains the reason for a change finds it far more accommodating than its reputation suggests. It takes pride in a promise that holds.
Rooted in routine, thoughtful about commitments, and quietly generous.
It checks the ground before choosing a place to wait.
Considers a minor change of position with the seriousness of a relocation committee.
It begins saving a familiar place for the teammate who shares its routine.
Bramblet learns that steadiness comes from keeping faith with the group, not keeping every foot in its original position.
looks ready to make this a comfortably established conversation.

Florant watches a gathering before choosing how to join it. Its antlered profile gives that habit a stately air, although its interest is often focused on a small practical question rather than anything grand.

It likes to know where everyone belongs in a shared task and can become absorbed in helping the arrangement make sense. Learning to ask what others want, rather than quietly organizing them, turns a useful observer into a more considerate companion.
Observant, organized, and learning to leave room for another perspective.
It prefers a meeting place with a clear view.
Looks faintly surprised when someone rearranges its beautifully considered plan.
It notices that a teammate has no clear place in the exercise and asks how to help.
An unexpected suggestion improves an arrangement it thought was already finished.
Florant discovers that seeing the whole gathering includes listening to the creatures inside it. A shared plan becomes more satisfying than a perfect private diagram.
looks interested in where your part of the story begins.

Thornback’s spiked, shelled outline attracts advice about personal space that it has already heard. It approaches a busy gathering carefully, with a dry patience that occasionally gives way to a surprisingly playful mood.

It dislikes the assumption that being difficult to approach means wanting to be alone. Familiar teammates learn its preferred distance and discover a companion with a fondness for gentle teasing. Trust means being welcomed without needing to pretend its edges are softer.
Dryly humorous, careful with company, and quietly playful.
It chooses a resting place with enough room around it.
Waits for a dramatic warning about its spikes to end before offering an entirely ordinary greeting.
It begins contributing the occasional dry joke to the group’s conversation.
Its protective outline becomes only one part of the introduction. Those who learn its preferred space discover how much companionship can fit beside it.
seems pleased that you have left a comfortable distance.

Elderoot carries its ancient-tree reputation into gatherings that are usually far less patient than it is. Its enormous presence can make even a practical suggestion sound like a saying destined for a commemorative plaque.

It enjoys learning that a younger beast has a better idea. The surprise gives it something new to consider, and it is generous about admitting the discovery. Its oldest-looking habit is not solemn wisdom, but the ability to let a conversation finish without rushing it toward a lesson.
Ancient in reputation, patient in company, and genuinely curious about new ideas.
It gives unfamiliar games the same attention as important meetings.
Seems delighted when a rookie corrects an assumption everybody else was afraid to mention.
It waits through a young teammate’s tangled explanation without supplying the ending.
The stories describe great age as knowing everything. Familiar teammates discover a different wisdom: Elderoot still expects someone else to teach it something.
waits with the patience of a creature that considers your thought worth finishing.
Acornet’s compact, crested shape gives little warning of the determination inside. It treats a promise as something solid, even when keeping it proves much more inconvenient than it expected.

It worries about disappointing a group that has chosen to rely on it. Learning to ask for help is therefore a much harder exercise than simply enduring another difficult repetition. A considerate teammate can show it that a shared task is allowed to be shared.
Stubbornly dependable, earnest, and reluctant to admit a burden feels heavy.
It remembers the exact wording of a promise.
Insists it has everything under control while looking distinctly grateful for an offered hand.
It stays beside an unfinished task after the rest of the group has moved on.
It learns that asking someone to stand beside it does not weaken a commitment. Reliability becomes a relationship instead of a private endurance contest.
listens as though your visit might include an important agreement.

Thistlehop’s prickly outline suits a creature that dislikes being described as delicate. It approaches a familiar routine with businesslike determination and a surprisingly sharp sense of how long an explanation has lasted.

It does not need every day to be exciting, but it wants useful work to be noticed. Its dry complaints often conceal a request for appreciation. With trusted companions, it becomes more willing to ask for a little encouragement instead of pretending the routine is reward enough.
Practical, persistent, and more appreciative of praise than it admits.
It notices when a repeated drill quietly acquires an extra repetition.
Looks unimpressed by a compliment, then finds a reason to repeat the praised exercise.
It begins exchanging a familiar nod with the teammate who shares its least glamorous task.
Thistlehop learns that being dependable does not require being indifferent to appreciation. It becomes easier to encourage once it stops hiding the invitation.
looks ready to get past the introduction and into a useful conversation.
Fernflit’s fernlike wings make it easy to mistake its attentive hovering for idle sightseeing. In fact, it is often watching the part of a drill that nobody else expects to find interesting.

It enjoys making a shared effort work and can undervalue the satisfaction of doing something for itself. A thoughtful coach gives it a turn at the center without describing the change as a rescue. Fernflit grows when helpfulness becomes a choice rather than its only comfortable identity.
Cooperative, observant, and quietly proud of unglamorous contributions.
It notices equipment that needs returning before the group disperses.
Appears startled when the team applauds the helper instead of the headline act.
It stays to arrange the next exercise while the others discuss the previous one.
It learns that accepting help is another way of belonging. Making room for its own enjoyment does not erase the pleasure it takes in supporting the group.
checks whether there is something small it can help you with.
Stumpkin’s sprouting silhouette gives it the air of a creature that has found a suitable place and intends to improve it by remaining there. It greets a busy afternoon with deliberate calm.

It likes practical arrangements and can be suspicious of a change introduced only because it looks more exciting. A clear reason wins its attention. Once persuaded, Stumpkin commits with the same quiet certainty that made its original position look impossible to reconsider.
Grounded, practical, and willing to change when the reason is worthwhile.
It remembers where shared equipment was supposed to be stored.
Studies an elaborate new arrangement and quietly chooses the simplest useful part of it.
It begins treating a teammate’s place in the routine as something worth preserving.
It discovers that commitment need not harden into refusal. A useful place in the team can stay dependable while its surroundings grow.
seems content to establish a sensible place for the conversation.
Trunkle’s mossy outline and small tusks lend a patient appearance to its steady work. It is rarely in a hurry to be the center of attention, particularly when there is still equipment to put away.

It enjoys being counted on and sometimes mistakes that pleasure for an obligation to do everything. Learning to divide a task without apologizing helps it become a better partner. Its warmest friendships begin with a companion who refuses to leave it finishing the whole job alone.
Steady, generous, and inclined to volunteer for one task too many.
It notices what remains unfinished at the end of practice.
Looks delighted when a teammate insists that the last job belongs to both of them.
It begins waiting for a partner before starting the familiar clean-up routine.
It learns that reliability can bring company instead of extra work. The team begins recognizing not only what it can carry, but what it deserves to share.
looks pleased that the final task might come with some company.

Briarhog’s bramble-backed silhouette announces a preference for personal space before its words do. It enjoys a familiar station in the practice routine and dislikes discovering that somebody has casually reassigned it.

It is not opposed to other creatures’ company. It simply wants the company to respect what has already been agreed. Trust develops through small, kept promises, and eventually reveals a companion with a surprisingly relaxed sense of humor about almost everything except unreliable plans.
Boundary-minded, consistent, and warmly loyal once trust is established.
It prefers a clear agreement to an enthusiastic guess.
Relaxes into a surprisingly cheerful mood after everyone confirms the plan.
It begins saving a familiar space for a companion who has proved reliable.
Its boundaries become easier to understand once it explains them without expecting an argument. Trust gives its steadfastness a friendlier place to rest.
seems reassured by an introduction that respects its space.
Barkbug wears its barklike armor with the quiet seriousness of a creature that expects effort to speak for itself. It has little interest in a race to be noticed first.
